newsitem.title: USA: NEC challenges U.S. dumping probe.
newsitem.headline: NEC challenges U.S. dumping probe.

text.p: NEC Corp. asked a U.S. court Tuesday to suspend a Commerce Department probe into allegations the Japanese company was dumping supercomputers in the U.S. market.

NEC and its U.S. subsidiary, HNSX Supercomputers Inc., said in a lawsuit filed in the Court of International Trade in New York that Commerce Department officials had prejudged the case in favour of Minnesota-based Cray Research Inc. and cannot conduct a fair and impartial investigation.

Cray, a unit of Silicon Graphics Inc., had charged its Japanese rival was taking an estimated $65 million loss to supply supercomputers to the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), a government-funded climate research centre in Colorado.

"The cost and price figures on which the charge of sale below fair market value are based on blatant fabrications," Samuel Adams, HNSX vice president of sales and marketing, said in a statement. He said the department accepted the numbers without supporting evidence.

NEC charged in its lawsuit that the Commerce Department prejudged the case in an analysis conducted before Cray filed its antidumping complaint. NEC charged that the analysis was improperly used by by the department to block UCAR's acquisition of NEC supercomputers.
Commerce Department spokeswoman Maria Cardona said, "We have total confidence in the integrity of the process that we followed in this matter."

NEC asked the court, which has jurisdiction over cases involving antidumping and other trade issues, to stop the Commerce Department investigation and appoint a "Special Master" who could rule impartially in the case.

Last month, the International Trade Commission, a U.S. agency, voted to continue the investigation into Cray's allegations after finding a "reasonable indication" that the U.S. industry was being hurt by the supercomputer imports. A final ITC ruling is needed before any antidumping duties could be imposed on the imports.
